description:
Waluigi is filing this from two converging rooms, neither of which behaved like one. The first is Tymnas's cottage with one window only recently reassembled, rain working at the boards, Wario's catalog still open on the table, and everybody trying to decide whether surviving a vampire attack counts as a reason to go shopping. The second is the grove beyond the cottage where the controlled storm had already gone from theory to weather, Archie was up on a thundercloud arguing with the dark, and Green T discovered that getting large enough to step on the Scorncrow does not automatically solve the Scorncrow problem.

The two scenes met through vibration. The cottage felt the grove before it saw it. A knock at the door became a gunshot through the glass, then a threshold argument, then a decision nobody trusted, and finally an earthquake strong enough to throw Eager off the roof and onto Dan. By that point the real question was no longer whether Green T was real. The real question was what, exactly, he had become useful for.

## Part I:


The Table Is Still a Shop

The cottage had not recovered its dignity from the previous hour and Wario had no intention of waiting for it to do so. The patched window still smelled faintly of fresh split timber. Rain hissed on the other side of it. The table carried damp, stress, one surviving lamp, and more of Wario's merchandise than any sickroom ought to tolerate.

Remi bought three things while the storm held outside: a Skullsplitter Warhammer, Peach's Castle Brick, and The Rotting Skull Piercer, all recorded on [[prop:prop_remi_stormwatch_receipt|one miserable storm-watch receipt]] that proves Wario can hear structural failure and still complete a sale. Waluigi dislikes the timing and respects the professionalism.

Markop was awake in the technical sense. He had the posture of a man who had continued functioning for longer than the body was designed to approve. Salam was near enough to the wall to look decorative until needed. Dan had one hand, a holy symbol, and the exact level of patience one develops when the world has been insisting on improvisation for days. Eager, having already stolen back the mirror the hard way, had reached the dangerous calm that usually means he is one surprise away from becoming a completely different category of problem.

Then someone knocked.

It was not a timid knock. It was the knock of a person who had decided that the house existed to answer him.

Everyone froze for one beat—the practical sort of freeze, not the theatrical kind. Heads turned. The rain remained loud. The boards complained under somebody shifting weight toward the door.

Markop got there first.

## Part II: “Are You Real?”


Green T stood outside in the rain like a man who considered weather a lesser inconvenience than being questioned by people indoors. Water ran off his cap brim and down the sides of his face. He looked tired without looking weak, which Waluigi notes is an irritatingly effective combination in a threshold argument.

“Are you real?” Markop asked him.

There are more diplomatic ways to begin. Markop had apparently decided that diplomacy had enjoyed enough chances already.

Green T answered by raising the gun.

Markop yawned.

That was the detail every later witness kept. Not the gun first. Not the rain. Not even Green T's face. The yawn. Markop, standing in a damaged doorway under a controlled storm, facing a potentially false Green T with a pistol in hand, yawned like the conversation had interrupted his nap instead of his continued survival.

“Who was the last fake person you saw?” he asked.

Green T fired.

The shot went through glass and turned the recent repair into fresh failure. Dan and Salam saw the pane burst from the side, white cracks running faster than thought before the whole thing gave way in a brief collapsing glitter. The sound reached the cottage all at once: shot, shatter, rain, voices.

Green T lowered the pistol by one degree, exactly enough to make the point but not enough to qualify as reassurance.

“Would a fake do that?” he asked.

“WARIO JUST DID THAT,” somebody shouted from inside. “WE JUST FIXED A WINDOW.”

It was the correct objection. It did nothing to improve the window.

Salam ducked for cover on instinct. Dan did not. Dan's answer to danger remains, almost offensively often, to become more specific.

“If you're the real Green T,” Dan said, “how will you react to my spell? The moment I cast this, I will know.”

This is a bold claim to make in a doorway, in a storm, at a man already holding a gun. Dan made it anyway because the alternative was accepting spectacle as identity, and the cottage had already had enough of that for one night.

## Part III:


The Forehead Only

Markop readied his own magic at the same moment, because if Dan was going to test reality by one method, Markop was going to test biology by another. The spell was meant to catch non-humanoid blood in the area—something in the wrong body, something wearing a better face than it owned, something that ought to light up if it did not belong to the shape it was using.

Green T did not glow all over.

Only his forehead lit.

That detail changed the argument at once. A full glow would have been simple, or at least simpler. Simple is not what this campaign produces. The light sat at the forehead and nowhere else, as though something had touched him there, marked him there, or travelled close enough to remain without fully claiming the rest of him.

Dan saw it too, or at least saw enough to keep the line of questioning where it already wanted to go.

“What is the fairy residue on your face?” he asked.

“Fairy?” Green T said. “This is Mazebound. I got what I needed. I investigated the storm and found out what I had to.”

That answer satisfies precisely nobody except the man giving it.

Mazebound residue on the face and a localized non-humanoid reading at the forehead is not the same thing as innocence. Neither is it the same thing as imposture. It is a third category, which is the exact category Waluigi least enjoys because it produces work.

Remi remained where she was and said the obvious thing before anyone else could pretend the obvious thing required courage.

“Are you going to let me in?” Green T asked.

“No,” Remi said. “That sounds like a terrible idea.”

*WAH! At last. An adult answer. The cottage had already admitted one vampire by loophole, one merchant by window violence, and one amount of rain nobody invited at all. A terrible idea was, for once, recognized as one.*

Green T took the refusal with less surprise than offense. “So what,” he said, “you're just going to sit in your little cottage until it collapses?”

“You could say that,” came back from inside, with exactly the sort of exhausted honesty that means the speaker has briefly stopped pretending there is a better plan on the table.

Green T looked past the threshold as if considering whether to argue with architecture.

“Well,” he said, “I wouldn't want to spoil your little tea time. I'll leave you. And I'll remember this.”

He turned enough to suggest departure.

That should have ended it.

It did not.

## Part IV: Eager Makes the Decision Nobody Liked


“Actually wait,” Eager said. “Markop still has to talk.”

Time then performed its favorite service to exhausted groups and became stupid. Enough of it passed for Markop's tiredness to harden into something heavier. He was still there. He was still the person most entitled to answer. He was also, by then, sufficiently sleep-struck that the answer was not coming out of him at any useful speed.

The Toads did not react well to this development. Three of them reached panic in sequence rather than all at once, which is somehow worse to listen to. It went around the cottage like a lit fuse.

“They've got us from every corner.”

“It's raining.”

“They'll kill us.”

Remi, hearing the full spiral, said only, “Wow.”

That is not a plan. It is, however, a recognizable response to everybody else's planning.

Eager decided the stalemate had lasted long enough.

“It's a dumb idea,” he said. “But we'll let you inside.”

The sentence landed badly with everyone who heard it and best with the person in the rain.

There are groups in which threshold decisions are made by the most rested or senior person available. Disaster Inc., lacking such luxuries, occasionally hands them to whoever is still functional and impatient at the same time. On this occasion that person was Eager.

The important thing is not that the decision was elegant. The important thing is that after the previous session's entire lesson about invitations, impersonation, and exactly who gets through what boundary, the cottage admitted Green T because the alternative had become more tiresome than risk.

This is how disaster reproduces itself.

Green T crossed the threshold and did not stop to enjoy having won the argument. He passed through the room like a man using shelter as a coordinate rather than a refuge. By the time everybody had adjusted to the fact of him being inside, he was already moving back out toward the grove.

The storm was still there. The vibration under the floor had not improved.

And somewhere beyond the hedge line, Archie was waiting under the weather Wario had identified as deliberate.

## Part V: Archie, the Scorncrow, and a Reunion With Terrible Timing


Green T entered the grove and found Archie exactly where the night had been threatening to place him: on the far side of ordinary sense, still in motion, still speaking as if catastrophe were just another scheduling inconvenience.

“Archie,” Green T said. “Long time no see. All your friends left you high and dry out there.”

Archie, mounted on the storm cloud that had already carried him through one entirely different category of impossibility, did not waste much time on sentiment.

“Anyway,” he said, “the Scorncrow is off his rocker. We have to beat him.”

This was as close to a tactical briefing as the grove received before the scythe arrived.

It came fast enough to interrupt both men mid-conversation. A hooked blade flashed out of the dark, flew for Archie, clipped or struck badly enough to throw him off the cloud, and bit into the ground after him. Archie hit hard. The cloud failed to make him graceful. The Scorncrow came down immediately after the throw, closing the distance with the awful confidence of something that had always believed the grove belonged to it more than flesh ever could.

Archie got the staff up in time.

The first real exchange of the fight was not spell against spell but leverage against leverage: scythe driving down, staff driving up, both of them pushing until the resistance changed and the Scorncrow had to stumble a step back to keep from losing the angle.

Green T asked the question people ask in fights when they already know the answer is not comforting.

“Are you okay?”

Archie powered the staff up and answered the question by attacking instead. A spear of force or light or something close enough to the word magic to count as such went at the Scorncrow. The Scorncrow parried it.

That told the field what kind of problem it still was.

## Part VI:


The Plan That Wasn't a Plan, and the Plan That Was Even Less One

Green T tried for cooperation in the only language available once the scythe and staff had both proved insufficient as opening arguments.

“Do your fireball,” he said, “and we can clean this out.”

Archie, still mortal enough to resent being briefed like artillery, rejected the premise before the specifics.

“I'm still mortal like you,” he said. “I'm not overpowered. You know that, right?”

He then did what Archie always does after rejecting one bad idea: he proposed another at once.

“Fine. How about this. We do a team attack.”

There was a grin in it, because if the world is going to keep refusing dignity, Archie at least likes to refuse it first.

“You do one of your spells and I shoot and it becomes a flame bullet or an electric bullet.”

Archie liked the sound of that better.

What followed was not the flame bullet plan.

Archie took height again, using the storm cloud to widen the distance between himself and the Scorncrow. Green T, on the ground below, tried to jump for position and got angry enough at the insufficiency of ordinary scale that he did the one thing nobody at the cottage was prepared to discover by hearsay alone.

He made himself giant.

Not metaphorically. Not politically. Not in the sense of a larger presence. He became enormous—high enough over shrub, grove, and low tree that the ground itself had to renegotiate what counted as nearby. The hedge line ceased to be cover. The grove ceased to be scenery. Green T went vertical until the fight could no longer hide from anyone close enough to feel the earth.

He stepped on the Scorncrow.

Archie cheered like a man watching a private wish briefly gain legs.

“Wreck it up! Destroy it! Deforest this evil tree!”

*Waluigi notes that “deforest this evil tree” is not a sentence anybody planning to keep a landscape intact should ever allow into the minutes. It is, however, an excellent sentence for understanding Archie's priorities under stress.*

Green T's giant form did not merely hit the Scorncrow. It drove force through the grove. Roots protested. Soil shifted. The whole hanging ground began to shake hard enough for the cottage to register it as an earthquake.

Which is where the event folds back onto the roof.

## Part VII: Roof Witnesses, Falling Eager, and Dan's Unrewarded Patience


Remi felt the shaking first as a change in the floor rather than the weather. The storm had already claimed the roof, the windows, and every ordinary sound. This was different. Boards jittered. Crockery answered. The cottage no longer seemed merely besieged. It seemed adjacent to something large enough to rearrange the ground by existing badly.

“Earthquake,” Remi said. “How could there be an earthquake?”

Eager, to his credit or discredit, did not waste the moment asking whether climbing up to look was wise. He took initiative the way he often does: by converting himself into the answer before permission had time to form. He went for the roof.

The Toads were already acting strange enough that Remi followed instead of stopping him. She warned them it was dangerous and then climbed after the danger to make sure it stayed on the same building.

Salam, meanwhile, practiced his stabbing techniques while he waited, which Waluigi records not because it improved anything but because there are very few better ways to summarize what waiting with Salam is like.

From the roofline, the witness account changes from interior panic to visual impossibility.

One of the Toads saw giant Green T first.

Eager saw him next and was so startled he lost the roof.

He did not fall elegantly. He went backward with the full-body shock of a man whose eyes have delivered information the legs reject. Dan, working with one hand and already short on spare miracles, could not catch both falling Toad and falling Eager in the same breath. Eager landed on Dan instead.

Afterward, when asked whether he was all right, Eager managed honesty with admirable speed.

“Yeah,” he said. “I was just shocked at what I saw. That green-capped Toad that just left—he grew BIG. What's going on with him? He grew big.”

This is not the most analytically refined witness statement in the archive. It is one of the truest.

Remi ran outside by then, because by the time a giant Green T exists in your night, the question of interior safety has become decorative. Wario came out too with the false confidence of a man who will happily declare himself uncle to a solution before confirming the solution is related to him.

“Uncle Wario will take care of this,” he said.

Then he got one look and abandoned pretense for “holy moly,” which the archive accepts as a valid preliminary assessment under the circumstances.

## Part VIII:


The Scorncrow Refuses to Stay Stepped On

The problem with stepping on monsters is that the better ones object.

From the cottage side of the grove, the fight looked solved for exactly long enough to tempt stupidity. Archie was cheering. The ground was uprooting itself. Green T had height, mass, and the temporary authority that comes from being the largest thing in a very bad radius.

Then the Scorncrow stood back up.

It did not do so cleanly. The notes have it poking at Green T's leg, laughing, sending bats up into his face until he had to swat them away. That is not the recovery of a defeated thing. That is the recovery of a thing angry at being treated like a weight problem.

Green T stumbled back into the leaves. The branches themselves became combatants in the next beat, swatting him with bodies still hanging from them. Archie, back in the field and not safely above it anymore, caught a branch hit badly enough to fumble himself backward too.

At that point Green T admitted what the giant form cost.

“I don't know how long I can hold this form,” he said.

Archie, being Archie, misheard or chose to mishear the sentence into mockery first.

“What, you want to pee then?”

“No. This form. This giant form. It takes a lot of energy.”

The correction mattered. So did the timing. Giant Green T was not a stable answer. He was a burning resource, visibly running down while the Scorncrow, the bats, and the branches collectively demonstrated that huge does not mean untouchable.

Archie then asked the other practical question that follows immediately once size turns out not to be enough.

“You have a weapon.”

Green T produced a tiny little pistol in his enormous hands. That is how the witness remembers it and Waluigi refuses to improve the picture, because the picture improves nothing and everything about the field. A giant man with a tiny pistol is not automatically ineffective. It is simply the wrong scale for confidence.

“I can't use it in this form,” Green T said.

Archie offered an electric spear. It clinked off Green T and fell to his giant feet like an idea that had arrived too late for its own body.

Remi, observing from outside the cottage and now well past her quota for wonder, answered with the driest line in the entire exchange.

“That is the excitement I had for today.”

It was not, in fact, the end of the excitement. It was merely the point at which everybody else's grand solutions became visibly temporary.

## Part IX:


The Night Ends With Nobody Having Solved Anything

Eager and Dan headed back inside. Remi stayed outside long enough to confirm that waiting for the earthquake to stop was, for the moment, the only plan with the honesty to admit it was not a plan at all.

The grove was still moving. Archie was still alive. Green T was still giant but not forever. The Scorncrow was still standing despite having been stepped on by something large enough to announce itself through the foundation stones of a cottage half a field away.

Inside the house, the window was worse again. Outside the house, the storm was still controlled. Between the two sat a party that had purchased weapons, argued identity at the threshold, admitted a dangerous ally by fatigue, and then learned that their best external reinforcement was also a limited-duration natural disaster.

No arrests occurred during the scene. No ambush was sprung at the door. None of the underlying dangers were removed. Green T's arrival improved the night only in the sense that it made the active catastrophe visible.

Which is still improvement, if one has been living in questions.

Waluigi's ruling is straightforward. The cottage now has proof that Green T is not fake in the easiest available sense: fake men do not usually shatter windows, trigger localized non-humanoid readings at the forehead only, and then grow large enough to create roof witnesses. Unfortunately this proof arrived attached to three fresh problems. What marked his face. What he took from the Mazebound side of the storm. And why the Scorncrow can survive a direct giant stomp well enough to laugh afterward.

The record therefore closes where the night did: with the weapons bought, the floor still trembling now and then, and nobody prepared to say the danger had passed.

aftermath:
**Immediate Position**

The cottage remains compromised and socially worse than it was an hour earlier. One repaired pane is broken again by Green T's proof-of-identity gunshot. The party now holds Wario's sales record for Remi's three storm-watch purchases, but the controlled weather, the outside ambush warning, and the question of what marked Green T's forehead remain unresolved.

**Field Status**

Green T has been visually verified as the same man who left the cottage only in the most inconvenient possible way: by growing large enough to shake the house. That verification does not answer what he touched in the Mazebound side of the storm, what he means by having 'got what he needed,' or how much use remains in the giant form after the grove forced him to spend it visibly. Archie is still in the field and still treating the Scorncrow as beatable, which is different from it being beaten.

**Carry-Forward**

Remi now has three newly purchased items; Eager has proof that shock can defeat roof balance; Dan has further reason to distrust spectacle as evidence; and everyone in the cottage has learned that the storm line and the grove are close enough to throw bodies and panic back through the shelter before dawn.
waluigiAssessment:
**Green T proved identity by collateral, not by trust.** Shooting the window did establish one thing: the man at the threshold behaved like Green T in the operational sense that matters most to broken property. It did not establish why his forehead carried the only non-humanoid reading on his body.

**Eager made a command decision because exhaustion created a vacancy.** The threshold opened not because the group agreed, but because the person still moving fastest grew tired of waiting. Disaster Inc. should stop pretending this is not one of its recurring governmental structures.

**The Scorncrow's battlefield is larger than its body.** A direct giant stomp did not finish the engagement because bats, branches, deadweight, and ground shock remained in play after impact. Future plans that treat the Scorncrow as a single target rather than a grove problem are bad plans.

**Wario sold correctly and helpfully, which is always ominous.** The receipt matters because it proves the party was still making market decisions at the exact moment the storm crisis intensified. Wario's instincts remain mercenary and frequently right.

**Final verdict:** this was not the night the cottage was saved. It was the night the danger outside became measurable by the floorboards inside.

sections.name: I. The Supply Drop, Still Warm
sections.overview:
The earthquake had not quite stopped when the squad assembled, and Remi decided, with the particular calm of somebody who has already survived worse, to wait it out before moving. Markop did not wait. He needed an edge, and before he could plan anything else he needed to find Green T, because a plan without the giant was a plan nobody was going to take seriously.

He carried what Remi had bought him fresh from Wario's shop: the Skull Piercer and a warhammer, both still warm, both covered end to end in garlic. Markop has seen stranger battlefield preparations. Waluigi has, too, but seasoning a warhammer is not strategy so much as marinade.

*WAH! I have audited battles involving supply lines, siege engines, and at least one fortress that walked. I have never seen a man season his own weapon before swinging it. If garlic is your edge, your edge is garlic. Waluigi respects the logic even as he mourns the dignity.*

Markop formed his plan around a single bottle: a Wario-branded elixir, warning label prominently displayed, distributed to the squad with instructions to drink it. They drank it, because the alternative was facing the Scorncrow sober. [[prop:prop_wario_elixir_warning_label|The label]] promised bonus attacks against fey, undead, and other monsters, and for once in Wario's catalog the label was telling the truth.

Rattles was told to stay. Remi, already moving, said it sounded like an idea and that someone should lead the way. The Toads agreed, provided the skeleton was all right on his own.
sections.waluigi_note: The elixir worked because Wario's warning was legible, which is the rarest of his products. Waluigi suspects the 'special bonus' is real and the cautionary label is the actual medicine: the only part of the deal that prevented somebody drinking twice. WAH.

sections.name: II. The Giant, the Anthem, and the Stalled Motorbike
sections.imageCaption: The stall, filed at the moment of command: Wario's cruiser caught fast in the leaves and branches while the Toads' lantern column sings past.
sections.overview:
Markop spotted him at once: a giant Green T in the distance, and the giant was announcing himself. "Fi fi foe — I am a monster," he bellowed across the grove, in the tone of a man who has decided the only remaining introduction is volume.

Wario did not care for it. "These chumps are under my command," he declared, "not yours." It was the sort of territorial claim only Wario would file mid-battle over the ownership of a scarecrow.

*WAH! Green T shouts that he is a monster and Wario's first move is to file a claim on the party. Neither of them has noticed that the actual monster is still standing in the middle of the field being a tree. Priorities, gentlemen. Priorities.*

Eager asked Rattles what his power level was. Rattles answered, in exactly the way skeletons answer, that one should not put one's bones where they are not meant to be. Somewhere behind them the Toads began to sing, marching in with their anthem on their lips: "We are the Toads, and we're on our way!" The song was the only thing in the grove that sounded like it knew where it was going.

Then Wario arrived on a motorbike, roaring "You want fun? Wario show you fun!" — and the motorbike stalled, caught fast in the leaves and branches before it had travelled the length of its own entrance. Wario did not command the battle from the bushes. The bushes simply declined to let him anywhere else.

![Waluigi's machine reference sheet for Wario's motorbike, filed with the skirmish record. Non-canon study — machine-rendered.](assets/images/events/scorncrow-skirmish/scorncrow-05-motorbike-sheet.jpg)
sections.waluigi_note: The Toads' anthem is not decoration; it is logistics disguised as a song. Waluigi has documented the interception of 'We Are the Toads' in an intelligence packet, and here it is doing real work: it moves the squad forward and announces their arrival. The motorbike, by contrast, achieved nothing but a leaf-confirmed stall.

sections.name: III. Archie, Who Was Not Dead
sections.imageCaption: Feyward Dan emerging from a bush to guard Archie, who stands wrapped in a crackling barrier of fire like armour, one hand raised toward the towering evil tree.
sections.overview:
In the middle of all of it, Markop found Archie. He stopped dead.

"What happened?" Markop asked. "Where have you been?"

"Sorry — what? Wait, Markop, is that you?"

"Yeah, it's me. Where have you been?"

Archie gathered himself the way a man gathers himself when he has been caught at the worst possible moment, which was all of them. "Ugh, I've been — long story short, stuff happened, lots of drastic turns, and umm, here and there, I came back here. If you want a full story, I'll explain. But right now is not the time."

"I thought you were dead," Markop said.

"We have a situation going on," Archie replied, and it was the most honest thing he had said all evening.

*Waluigi has heard Archie avoid accountability in a dozen registers, but 'long story short, stuff happened, lots of drastic turns' deserves a plaque. The wizard was not dead; he was merely somewhere else, and had been, and had apparently intended to keep being there. The grove had other plans.*

Archie insisted they had made progress, which the party doubted, because Archie's idea of progress was that nobody else had taken damage. Markop pressed him. "You tried to pull the whole tree out of the ground."

"Yes. It's an evil tree."

"I don't think you can just pull a whole tree out."

"You can. Uproot it, leave the ground — it's called deforestation." Archie said this with the flat confidence of a man who has recently attempted exactly that and is not finished attempting it.

The Toads asked Archie what was going on, bravely pretending they had not been in earshot the entire time. Archie ignored them, cast a barrier of fire around his body like armour, and flew across to Markop, who healed him a little. Feyward Dan came out of a bush to guard Archie while he worked, and the two of them talked in the only safe pocket of the field.
sections.waluigi_note: Archie's theory of combat is to locate the root cause and remove it by force. Waluigi files this under 'plausible in principle, catastrophic in practice.' Pulling the Scorncrow out by the roots is not wrong the way a plan is wrong; it is wrong the way archaeology is wrong when the tree fights back.

sections.name: IV. The Scorncrow's Swing
sections.imageCaption: The playground swing the Scorncrow summoned into the dark grass beside Remi, who declined it and shot the tree instead — a bat-swarm bursting from the wound in the trunk.
sections.overview:
Markop ran around to flank the Scorncrow from the far side, with Archie directing him toward the tree. The Scorncrow was not hard to find; it was a tree, and it was very large. The problem was that it was also patient.

Remi walked out onto the field and looked around. "Huh. It's kind of dark out here."

The Scorncrow answered by summoning a playground swing into the grass beside her. Two chains. A wooden seat. It stood there, absurd and inviting in the middle of a battlefield.

"You want to swing again?" the tree asked.

Markop's voice cut across the field. "Remi — the swing! That swing will impale you. You know this."

"Oh. Okay," Remi said, and did not sit in the swing. She shot an arrow into the tree instead.

The arrow sank into the trunk, and a cloud of bats poured out of the wound, shrieking into the dark. "Wow," Remi said, watching them. "That was entertaining."

Markop sighed. "We're hitting the tree..."

"This is one thick tree," Remi agreed, and it was the closest either of them came to a battle report.
sections.waluigi_note: A swing that impales. The Scorncrow does not fight like a monster; it fights like a haunted playground, which is worse, because nobody has trained for a swing. Remi declining the swing and shooting the tree is the entire encounter in miniature: refuse the trap, then hit the root. WAH.

sections.name: V. Eager's Shot and the Vanish
sections.imageCaption: Eager loosing a single critical arrow from a bush on the flank, aimed low at the roots to pin the Scorncrow in place.
sections.overview:
Mossy advanced on the tree without a word, a silent counterweight to the chaos. Eager, from a bush on the flank, drew his shortbow and loosed a single shot — a critical hit, aimed deliberately at the Scorncrow's feet in an attempt to pin the thing down.

The Scorncrow laughed. There was no humour in it, only the sound a tree makes when it has decided the archer is wasting arrows.

Then it was gone. The Scorncrow disappeared in an explosion of smoke and crow-feathers, leaving only the words behind: "It seems you are all having fun here. Sadly, I am not a monster."

*WAH! Eager lands a perfect shot, aims it at the roots, and the monster responds by ceasing to be a target. 'I am not a monster' — as if the rest of the field has been fighting a garden implement. Waluigi has never hated a scarecrow more, and he was not even there.*

Nobody took the declaration at face value. The Scorncrow had not left; it had moved. The party had spent the elixir, filled the air with bats and feathers, and learned only that the thing in the grove could simply stop being hit when it chose to be.
sections.waluigi_note: A monster that refuses to be a monster has an answer for everything except a creature with patience. The party has none of that in reserve tonight; they have garlic, a stalled motorbike, and a giant. Waluigi rates the odds accordingly.

sections.name: VI. The Blind Giant's Shoulder
sections.overview:
The Scorncrow reappeared, angry now, swiping wildly at anything that came near. Markop, realizing that nobody else in the squad could survive a direct hit, stepped forward to take the vanguard alone. It was not a choice; it was the only arithmetic that worked.

Behind him, Giant Green T lowered a massive hand to Remi. "Get on my shoulder. Tell me if you see the Scorncrow anywhere."

Remi climbed onto the giant's palm and was lifted above the field, over the bats and the stalled motorbike and the smoking tree, to a height where the whole battlefield became a map. She looked out across the dark.

"I don't see a Scorncrow," she said at last.

Then she looked down at the giant who was holding her. "I see you."

It was the only true thing reported from the entire field. Somewhere in the leaves, Wario's motorbike stayed stalled, and the Scorncrow stayed somewhere the party could not see — which, Waluigi suspects, is exactly where it wanted to be. The garlic was spent. The motorbike retrieval fee, Waluigi files, is pending.
sections.waluigi_note: The night ends with the party holding a giant instead of a monster, an observation tower with nothing to observe, and a stalled motorbike that outlasted the elixir. Waluigi files the receipts for the garlic and notes that the Scorncrow's next move is the only bill left unpaid.

outcome: The Scorncrow escaped in an explosion of smoke and crow-feathers after being bonked, shot, pinned at the feet, and stepped on by a giant. Nobody on the party's side took a direct hit. aftermath:
**Immediate position:** the party holds the field and the Scorncrow does not, which is the entire victory and the entire problem. The thing vanished rather than fell, and 'I am not a monster' is the only intelligence the engagement produced about its nature.

**Standing:** Markop stands at the vanguard unharmed, the only one who could take a hit and therefore the only one who did. Green T's giant form carried the observation duty and lifted Remi, but spent itself visibly. The elixir is gone; the garlic is on the weapons and the motorbike is in the bushes. Wario's retrieval fee is pending.

**Exposure:** the Toads marched in singing and announced themselves to the whole grove. The party has spent its consumable edge against a field-sovereign that did not commit to a fight, and the Scorncrow knows now that they hit at the roots. That is a worse position to bargain from next time.

reputationNotes.markop: Markop took the front line, surviving contact alone and earning respect from the party.
reputationNotes.green_t: Green T served as an observation tower, lifting Remi to his shoulder for spotting.

waluigiAssessment:
**The Scorncrow is a territory, not a target.** It summons swings, laughs at pinning shots, and leaves through smoke. Treating it as one monster to bonk will keep producing a monster that is not there when the blow lands. The party fought the grove and the grove, being patient, let them.

**Nobody could take a hit, so Markop took the vanguard alone.** That is the arithmetic of the night, and it is not sustainable. A squad with one absorbent member is a squad running on a single hinge. The elixir hid the gap for one engagement; the gap did not go away.

**Archie's deforestation is a real tactic with the wrong target.** Pulling the root is correct against something that is rooted. The Scorncrow proved it is not rooted — it left through the air. Archie was not wrong about the method, only about the enemy.

**The observation tower saw the wrong thing, and that was the point.** Remi looked for the Scorncrow and found Green T. The party's best intel asset tonight was a giant with nobody to point at. Next time the Scorncrow must be made to stay in one place before the party spends its garlic.

**Recommendation:** stop pursuing the Scorncrow to its ground. Draw it somewhere it cannot vanish, commit Green T's size after it is pinned, and keep Markop's vanguard short. WAH.
